decks.title: Development — Part 1: Goals, Income and Averages
goals: Explain why different people have different and sometimes conflicting development goals
Explain why non-income goals such as security, equality and freedom matter
Calculate and interpret average (per capita) income, and state its limitations
Describe how the World Bank compares countries

slides.heading: Development
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what **development** means to different people, why **income is not the only goal**, and how countries are compared using **average income**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: what people want, different and conflicting goals, income and other goals, national development, and average income
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Namaste! What would make your life better? A bigger home, a good school, a safe street, a job you enjoy? Your answer is your idea of development. In economics, development is about how people's lives can improve. In this part we see that different people want different things, that money is important but not everything, and how economists compare whole countries using average income.

slides.heading: Development begins with aspirations
slides.body_md: Every person has hopes for a better life. **Development** is about these aspirations: what people want and how their lives can improve.

rows: What do people want from life?
Do all people want the same things?
No: goals depend on each person's situation
With indicators: income, health, education, and more

visual.alt: Table of three questions about development: what people want, whether everyone wants the same, and how progress can be measured

slides.narration: Development is not a single thing that a government delivers. It starts with ordinary people and their hopes. A student wants good teachers; a farmer wants water for his fields; a nurse wants a safe journey home after a night shift. Economists then ask: can we measure whether lives are getting better? Keep these three questions in mind; they shape the whole chapter.

slides.heading: Different people, different goals

rows: A daily-wage construction worker in a city
Work every day, fair wages, a safe place to live
A farmer who depends on rain
Irrigation, timely credit, a fair price for crops
A young woman from a well-off family
Freedom to choose her studies and career, equal treatment
A fishing family on the coast
Clean seas, safe boats, a market for their catch
A family in a valley where a dam is planned
Keeping their land, homes and way of life
A shopkeeper in a small town
Good roads, steady electricity, customers with money to spend

visual.alt: Table of six people and their development goals: a construction worker wants regular work and fair wages, a rain-fed farmer wants irrigation and fair prices, a young woman wants freedom and equal treatment, a fishing family wants clean seas, a valley family wants to keep its land, and a shopkeeper wants roads, power and customers

slides.narration: Read down this table and notice how the goals change with each person's situation. The worker wants regular work. The farmer wants water. The young woman wants freedom. The valley family simply wants to keep its home. None of them is wrong. That is the first big idea of this chapter: different people have different development goals, because their lives are different.

slides.heading: When goals collide
slides.body_md: One group's progress can be another group's **loss**.

nodes.label: Gainers: towns get electricity; plains get irrigation; industries get power
Losers: valley families lose land, homes and their way of life

visual.alt: Flow: a large dam gives towns electricity, plains irrigation and industries power, but valley families lose land, homes and their way of life

slides.narration: Sometimes goals do not just differ; they clash. A dam can light up towns and water farms in the plains, but it can flood the villages in the valley. A factory brings jobs, but its waste may spoil a river that fishing families depend on. When you write about development, always ask: development for whom, and at whose cost?

slides.heading: Quick check: conflicting goals
slides.body_md: A factory beside a river creates jobs, but fishing families downstream want the river clean. What does this show?
slides.narration: Two groups, one river, two different goals. What is the general lesson?

slides.heading: Income and other goals
columns:
**Material goals (income)**

- More income, regular work, better wages
- Things money can buy: food, clothes, a house, a vehicle

**Non-material goals**

- Equal treatment, freedom, security, respect
- A safe environment, especially for women working outside the home
- Things money alone cannot buy
slides.narration: Most people want more income, and that is fair: money buys food, clothes and a home. But people also want things money cannot buy on its own: to be treated with respect, to feel safe, to be free to make choices. If a woman earns well but is harassed on the way to work, has her life truly improved? Development means both kinds of goals.

slides.heading: Two job offers
slides.body_md: Meena (an imagined graduate) chooses **Job 2**. She is weighing **security, family and freedom** along with income.

visual.alt: Table comparing two imagined job offers: Job 1 pays more but is far away, insecure and has long hours; Job 2 pays a little less but is near family, secure and leaves time to study

slides.narration: Here is a simple test of the idea. Meena has two job offers. One pays more, but it is far away, insecure and leaves no time to study. The other pays a little less, but it is near her family, secure and flexible. Many people would choose the second. Not because money does not matter, but because a good life has many parts. That is what economists call the quality of life.

slides.heading: Quality of life
bullets: Development is not only **how much** people earn, but **how well** they live.
A safe neighbourhood, clean air, freedom from discrimination and the chance to learn all raise the quality of life.
For women, paid work brings dignity only when the workplace and the journey are **safe**.
slides.narration: Put the two ideas together and you get the quality of life. Income raises it, but so do safety, respect, freedom and a clean environment. That is why two families with the same income can have very different lives. Remember this phrase in your answers: development is about the quality of life, not just the quantity of income.

slides.heading: Quick check: two job offers
slides.body_md: If Meena chooses Job 2, what is she showing?
slides.narration: She gave up some income. What did she gain in return?

slides.heading: From people to nations
slides.body_md: If people want different things, how can we say one **country** is more developed than another? We need some common characteristics to compare.

nodes.label: A country is a collection of people

visual.alt: Flow: people have different goals, a country is a collection of people, so to compare countries we need a common measure, and income is one important measure

slides.narration: Now we move from people to whole countries. If everyone wants different things, comparing countries seems impossible. Economists solve this by picking a few important characteristics that most people value. The first one they usually pick is income, because more income generally means people can have more of the things they need. But which income: the country's total, or the income per person?

slides.heading: Why we use average income
slides.body_md: Countries have **different populations**, so their **total income** says little about what a typical person earns.

visual.alt: Table: imagined Bigland has a total income of one crore crore rupees and 200 crore people, so 50,000 rupees per person; imagined Smallland has 20 lakh crore rupees and 10 crore people, so 2 lakh rupees per person

math: \text{Per capita income} = \dfrac{\text{Total income of the country}}{\text{Total population}}
slides.narration: Look at the two imagined countries. Bigland's total income is five times Smallland's, so it seems richer. But Bigland also has twenty times as many people. Divide total income by population and Smallland's people earn four times as much each. That is why we use average income, also called per capita income. It tells us what an average person has.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: calculating per capita income
slides.body_md: Question: *An imagined state has a total annual income of ₹6,00,000 crore and a population of 4 crore. Find its per capita income.*
bullets: Step 1 — Write the formula: per capita income = total income ÷ population.
Step 2 — Check the units: both figures are in crore, so the crores cancel.
Step 4 — Answer with the unit: **₹1,50,000 per person per year**.
Step 5 — Interpret: this is what each person would get if the state's income were shared equally, which it never is.

visual.alt: Table of working: formula, total income divided by population; substitution, six lakh crore rupees divided by four crore; answer, one lakh fifty thousand rupees per person per year

slides.narration: Calculations in this chapter are simple, but marks are lost on units. Write the formula first. Notice that both numbers are in crore, so the crores cancel, leaving six lakh divided by four. The answer is one lakh fifty thousand rupees per person per year. Always finish with one line of meaning: this is an average, not what every person actually earns.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: same average, different lives
slides.body_md: Two imagined villages, four families each, monthly income in ₹ thousand: **P** = 18, 22, 19, 21; **Q** = 4, 6, 5, 65.
bullets: Step 2 — Averages: both are $\dfrac{80}{4} = 20$, i.e. ₹20,000.
Step 3 — Look at the spread: in P everyone is close to ₹20,000; in Q three families earn ₹4,000–₹6,000.
Step 4 — Conclude: the average **hides inequality**; most people would rather live in P.

visual.alt: Bar chart of monthly family incomes: Village P families earn 18, 22, 19 and 21 thousand rupees; Village Q families earn 4, 6, 5 and 65 thousand; a dashed line marks the same average of 20 thousand for both
visual.caption: Same average, very different distribution.

slides.narration: This is the most important limitation of averages, so learn it with an example of your own. Both villages have exactly the same average income. But look at the bars. In Village P, every family is close to the average. In Village Q, one rich family pulls the average up while three families are poor. An average tells you nothing about how income is shared. That is why we need other measures too.

slides.heading: Quick check: why averages?
slides.body_md: Why do we use average income rather than total income to compare countries?
slides.narration: Think about what happens when two countries have very different numbers of people.

slides.heading: How the World Bank compares countries
slides.body_md: The World Bank groups countries mainly by **income per person** (gross national income per capita, in US dollars). The thresholds are revised every year.

visual.alt: Table of the World Bank income groups, high, upper-middle, lower-middle and low income, with India placed in the lower-middle-income group

slides.narration: International organisations need a quick way to compare countries. The World Bank uses income per person and sorts countries into four groups, from high income to low income. The exact dollar limits change every year, so you do not need to memorise them. Just remember that India is a lower-middle-income country, and that this method has the same weakness as any average: it ignores how income is shared.

slides.heading: Quick check: the World Bank's yardstick
slides.body_md: Which criterion does the World Bank mainly use to classify countries?
slides.narration: One number per country, related to money. Which is it?

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Aspirations for a better life; different for different people
Development for one can be destructive for another (dams, factories)
Income matters, but so do security, equality, freedom and respect: quality of life
Total income ÷ population; makes countries comparable
Averages hide how income is distributed
Groups countries by income per person; India is lower-middle income

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: development as aspirations, conflicting goals, income and other goals, per capita income, its limitation and the World Bank classification

slides.narration: Here is Part 1 in a nutshell. Development means different things to different people, and goals can clash. Income is important, but so are security, respect and freedom: together they make up the quality of life. To compare countries we use per capita income, total income divided by population. It is useful, but it hides inequality. In Part 2 we look at better ways to measure development.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Per capita income: write the formula, show the division, give the unit (₹ per person per year).
Always pair "average income" with its limitation: it **hides distribution**.
Development goals questions: name the person, the goal and why it suits their situation.
For conflicting goals, give one project with a **gainer** and a **loser**.
Non-income goals: security, equality, freedom, respect, a safe environment.
Do not memorise World Bank dollar limits; they change each year.
slides.narration: Three tips for this part. In any calculation, show the formula and the unit. Whenever you mention average income, add its limitation, because examiners look for it. And when you discuss development goals, tie each goal to the person's situation. Making up your own clear example is perfectly acceptable, and often scores better than a memorised one.

decks.title: Development — Part 2: Public Facilities, HDI and Sustainability
goals: Compare states using infant mortality, literacy and attendance as well as income
Explain the role of public facilities such as health care, schools and the PDS
Explain why sustainability matters, using groundwater and crude oil examples
Write a data-based 5-mark answer that earns full marks

slides.heading: Beyond income
slides.body_md: Part 2 — why **income is not enough**, how **public facilities** change lives, how the **Human Development Index** measures progress, and why development must be **sustainable**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: what money cannot buy, health and education indicators, comparing states, the Human Development Index, and sustainability
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: Welcome back. In Part 1 we used income to compare countries and found its weakness: averages hide inequality. But there is a deeper problem. Many things that make life good cannot be bought by a family on its own. In this part we meet better indicators, see how public facilities can matter more than income, learn about the Human Development Index, and ask whether today's development can last.

slides.heading: What a family's income cannot buy
slides.body_md: For many goods and services, **collective provision** is cheaper and works better than each family arranging its own.

rows: Schools and public health centres in every area

visual.alt: Table: food, clothes, a phone, furniture and tuition can be bought individually, while neighbourhood security, a pollution-free environment, protection from infectious diseases, and schools and health centres are best provided collectively

slides.narration: Money can buy a phone or a new shirt. But can one family buy clean air for its street, or protection from malaria? Can it hire its own police force? These things work only when they are provided for everyone together, usually by the government or the community. So a region's development depends a lot on its public facilities, not just on how much its people earn.

slides.heading: Three indicators beyond income

rows: Children who die before the age of one, per 1,000 live births in a year
Literate people as a share of the population aged 7 and above
Children of an age group (e.g. 14–15 years) attending school, as a share of all children of that age group

visual.alt: Table of indicators: infant mortality rate, deaths before age one per 1,000 live births, where low is good; literacy rate, literate share of people aged seven and above, where high is good; net attendance ratio, share of children of an age group attending school, where high is good

slides.narration: Here are three indicators that look beyond income. The infant mortality rate tells us how many babies die before their first birthday, out of every thousand born alive. It is a sharp test of health care. The literacy rate tells us how many people aged seven and above can read and write. And the net attendance ratio tells us how many children of a given age are actually in school. Remember: for IMR, lower is better.

slides.heading: Comparing three states
slides.body_md: State P is richest, but State Q does far better on **health and education**.

visual.alt: Table of three imagined states: State P has the highest per capita income of 2.4 lakh rupees but an IMR of 28; State Q has 1.6 lakh rupees, the lowest IMR of 8, literacy of 94 per cent and attendance of 90 per cent; State R has 70 thousand rupees, IMR 32, literacy 70 per cent and attendance 55 per cent

slides.narration: Study this table carefully; questions like this appear in the board paper. If we looked only at income, State P would win easily. But State Q has far fewer infant deaths, more literate people and more children in school. In India, Kerala is a well-known real example: its income is not the highest, yet its infant mortality rate is among the lowest. Why? Mainly because of good basic health and education facilities.

slides.heading: Income does not decide health

x.label: Per capita income (₹ thousand per year)

visual.alt: Scatter plot of six imagined states: incomes from 70 to 300 thousand rupees and infant mortality rates from 8 to 32 with no simple pattern; a state with 160 thousand rupees has the lowest rate of 8, while a state with 240 thousand rupees has a rate of 28
visual.caption: Six imagined states. A higher income does not guarantee a lower infant mortality rate.

slides.narration: Each dot on this chart is an imagined state. If income alone decided health, the dots would fall in a neat line going down to the right. They do not. The state with the lowest infant mortality rate is in the middle of the income range, and one of the richest has a high rate. Public facilities like clinics, clean water and nutrition make the difference.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: reading a state comparison table
slides.body_md: Question: *Using the three-state table, which state is more developed? Give reasons.* (3 marks)
bullets: Step 1 — Read every row, not just income: P leads on income; Q leads on IMR, literacy and attendance.
Step 2 — Interpret: Q's IMR of 8 means far fewer babies die than in P (28) or R (32).
Step 3 — Explain the gap: Q probably has better **public facilities**: clinics, schools, a working PDS.
Step 4 — Judge: considering health and education with income, **Q is the most developed**; R needs the most help.

rows: Comparison using income and at least two other indicators
Correct interpretation of IMR (lower is better)

visual.alt: Marking plan: one mark for comparing income with at least two other indicators, one for correctly interpreting IMR, and one for a judgement with a reason

slides.narration: Data questions reward three habits. First, use more than one row of the table; a student who looks only at income misses the point. Second, interpret each indicator correctly: for infant mortality, a lower number is better. Third, end with a clear judgement and a reason. Examiners give the last mark for explaining why: here, better public facilities.

slides.heading: Quick check: lower income, better health
slides.body_md: Why might a state with lower income have a lower IMR and higher literacy?
slides.narration: What can a government provide that families cannot buy one by one?

slides.heading: Public facilities and the PDS
bullets: **Health centres** within reach, nurses visiting mothers and babies, and clean drinking water lower infant deaths.
**Schools** with midday meals keep children in class and raise literacy.
A well-run **public distribution system (PDS)**, where ration shops sell foodgrains at fair prices, improves the nutrition of poor families.
Where such facilities work well, people's **health and education** improve even if incomes are modest.
slides.narration: What exactly are these public facilities? A health centre within walking distance. A nurse who visits every new mother. A school that serves a hot meal, so children come every day. A ration shop that opens on time and sells grain at fair prices. None of these depends on one family's income. Together they explain why some states do much better on health and education than their income alone would predict.

slides.heading: The Human Development Index
slides.body_md: The **United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)** publishes the **Human Development Report**, which ranks countries by the **Human Development Index (HDI)**.

visual.alt: Flow: health measured by life expectancy, education measured by years of schooling, and income measured by per capita income combine into the Human Development Index, which runs from 0 to 1

slides.narration: The Human Development Index puts the ideas of this chapter into one number. It combines three things: how long people live, how much schooling they get, and their income. The score runs from zero to one, and countries are ranked by it every year by the United Nations Development Programme. Because it includes health and education, it gives a much fuller picture than income alone.

slides.heading: Key HDI terms

rows: The average number of years a newborn is expected to live
Average years of education received by adults
Years of education a child starting school can expect to receive
Income per person, adjusted so that it can be compared across countries (in US dollars)

visual.alt: Table of HDI terms: life expectancy at birth, mean years of schooling, expected years of schooling, and per capita income adjusted for comparison across countries

slides.narration: Learn these terms precisely. Life expectancy at birth is the number of years a newborn can expect to live on average. Schooling is measured in two ways: the years adults have actually studied, and the years a child starting school can expect to study. And the income figure is adjusted so that a dollar buys the same amount in every country. Precise definitions earn precise marks.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: interpreting HDI data
slides.body_md: Question: *Country L has the highest income of three imagined countries, but Country M ranks first on the HDI. Explain.*
bullets: Step 1 — Income: L USD 12,000 > M USD 9,000 > N USD 4,000 (per capita).
Step 2 — Health: life expectancy M 77 years, L 68, N 66.
Step 3 — Education: mean years of schooling M 10.0, L 6.5, N 5.0.
Step 4 — Combine: M leads by $77 - 68 = 9$ years of life and $10 - 6.5 = 3.5$ years of schooling; this outweighs L's income lead.
Step 5 — Conclude: the HDI rewards **health and education** as well as income.

visual.alt: Table of three imagined countries: L has the highest income but ranks second on HDI; M has lower income but the longest life expectancy and most schooling and ranks first; N ranks third

slides.narration: Here the richest country does not top the ranking. Why? Because the index cares about how long and how well people live. Country M's people live nine years longer and study three and a half years more than Country L's. In the answer, quote the numbers. A phrase like nine more years of life is far more convincing than saying M is healthier.

slides.heading: Quick check: HDI ranks
slides.body_md: Why can a country with lower income rank higher on the HDI?
slides.narration: What else does the index count besides income?

slides.heading: Can development last?
slides.body_md: **Sustainable development** meets present needs **without reducing the ability of future generations** to meet theirs.
bullets: Even **renewable** resources can be **overused** if we take more than nature replaces.
**Non-renewable** resources have fixed stocks that will be **exhausted**.
**Environmental damage** does not stop at national or state borders.
slides.narration: Suppose a region becomes richer by using up its water, forests and minerals. Is that development? Only for now. Sustainability asks a harder question: will our children be able to live as well as we do? Scientists, economists and many citizens now argue that development must protect resources and the environment. Let us look at two examples: groundwater and crude oil.

slides.heading: Groundwater: renewable but running out
slides.body_md: Groundwater is recharged by rain. When pumping exceeds recharge, the **water table falls**: overuse of a renewable resource.

visual.alt: Line chart for an imagined village: the depth to the water table grows from 12 metres in 2000 to 40 metres in 2025
visual.caption: Imagined figures: the deeper the water table, the more wells run dry.

slides.narration: Groundwater is renewable: rain soaks into the ground and refills it. But only at a certain speed. In this imagined village, more and more borewells pumped water for thirsty crops, and the water table sank from twelve metres to forty. The rain has not stopped; people are simply taking out more than it puts back. If this continues, the next generation of farmers will find their wells dry.

slides.heading: Crude oil: how long will it last?
slides.body_md: Crude oil is **non-renewable**: at the present rate of use, known reserves will run out unless new ones are found.

visual.alt: Table: an imagined country with 3,600 million barrels of reserves lasts 20 years at 180 million barrels a year, but only 10 years if production doubles to 360

slides.narration: Crude oil took millions of years to form, so its reserves are fixed. A simple calculation shows how long they will last: divide the reserves by the amount produced each year. If an imagined country has three thousand six hundred million barrels and produces one hundred and eighty million a year, it has twenty years. Double the production, and it has only ten. Faster use today means less for tomorrow.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a data-based 5-mark answer
slides.body_md: Question: *Study the three-state table. Which state is more developed? Justify with five points.* (about 120 words)
bullets: Step 1 — Point 1: compare **income** (P highest, R lowest), quoting figures.
Step 2 — Point 2: compare **IMR** and say lower is better (Q 8, P 28, R 32).
Step 3 — Point 3: compare **literacy and attendance** (Q highest on both).
Step 4 — Point 4: **explain** the pattern: Q's public facilities (health, schools, PDS).
Step 5 — Point 5: **judge**: Q is the most developed on a balanced view; R needs the most attention.

visual.alt: Marking plan for the data-based answer: one mark each for comparing income, comparing and interpreting IMR, comparing literacy and attendance, giving the reason of public facilities, and a balanced judgement

slides.narration: The economics section of the board paper often ends with a data-based long answer, so practise this pattern. Use every row of the table, quote numbers, and interpret each one. Then explain why the pattern exists and finish with a clear judgement. Five points, one mark each. The commonest mistake is to choose the richest state without looking at the other rows.

slides.heading: Quick check: groundwater
slides.body_md: Decide whether the assertion and the reason are true, and whether the reason explains the assertion.
slides.narration: Think about the speed of recharge and the speed of pumping.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2

rows: Security, clean environment, disease control, schools: cheaper and better for all together
IMR (lower is better), literacy rate (7+), net attendance ratio
Higher income does not guarantee better health and education; public facilities matter
UNDP; health (life expectancy), education (schooling), income; 0 to 1
Meet present needs without harming future generations; groundwater, crude oil

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 2: collective provision, indicators, comparing states, the HDI and sustainability

slides.narration: Part 2 in brief. Some of the most important things in life, like safety, clean air and health care, are best provided collectively. Indicators like infant mortality, literacy and attendance show how well people really live. The Human Development Index combines health, education and income. And development must be sustainable: if we exhaust groundwater or oil today, future generations pay the price.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 2
bullets: IMR: **lower is better**; literacy and attendance: higher is better.
Literacy rate is for people aged **7 and above**.
HDI = health + education + income; published by the **UNDP**.
Data questions: use every row, quote figures, explain, then judge.
Sustainability: give one **renewable** example (groundwater overuse) and one **non-renewable** example (crude oil).
Years left = reserves ÷ annual production; show the division.
slides.narration: Final tips. Never forget that a lower infant mortality rate is better; it is the most common slip in data questions. Learn who publishes the HDI and what it includes. In data-based answers, quote figures, explain the pattern and give a judgement. And for sustainability, show that you understand both kinds of resources: renewable ones that can be overused, and non-renewable ones that will run out.

notes.title: Development — Notes

sections.heading: 1. What development promises: different people, different goals
sections.body_md:
Development is about people's **aspirations** for a better life. Because people live in **different situations**, they have **different development goals**: a daily-wage worker wants regular work and fair wages; a rain-fed farmer wants irrigation and fair prices; a young woman may most value the freedom to choose her career; a family in a valley may want above all to keep its land.

Goals can also **conflict**: a dam may bring electricity and irrigation to towns and plains while submerging the homes and land of valley families; a factory may bring jobs but pollute a river that fishing families use. **One group's progress can be another group's loss.**

key_terms.definition_md: The process of improving people's lives in line with their aspirations; it means different things to different people.
Goals of different groups that cannot all be met at once, e.g. power from a dam versus homes in the valley.

rows: Young woman from a well-off family

visual.alt: Table of four people and their development goals

sections.heading: 2. Income and other goals
sections.body_md: Most people want **more income**, because it buys material things. But people also seek **non-material goals**: **equal treatment, freedom, security and respect**. For example, a person may choose a secure job near home over a higher-paid insecure job far away; women can gain from paid work only if the workplace and the journey are **safe**. Many things that improve life, such as a **pollution-free environment** or freedom from discrimination, cannot be bought by one family's income. Development is about the **quality of life**, not just income.

key_terms.definition_md: Goals such as security, freedom, equality and respect that income alone cannot buy.
How well people live, including income, health, education, safety, freedom and environment.

visual.alt: Table contrasting material income goals with non-material goals

sections.heading: 3. National development and average income
sections.body_md:
To compare **countries**, we choose characteristics most people value. **Income** is one: more income generally means more of the things people need. Because countries have **different populations**, we use **average income**, also called **per capita income**: total income divided by total population.

The **World Bank** classifies countries mainly by income per person (gross national income per capita, in US dollars) into high, upper-middle, lower-middle and low-income groups; the thresholds are revised every year. **India** is a **lower-middle-income** country.

**Limitation:** an average **hides the distribution** of income. Two places with the same average can be very different: in one everyone earns about the same; in another a few are rich and most are poor.

key_terms.definition_md: Total income of a country divided by its total population; also called average income.
How income is shared among the people of a place.

visual.alt: Bar chart of two imagined villages with the same average income of 20 thousand rupees: Village P incomes are 18, 22, 19 and 21 thousand; Village Q incomes are 4, 6, 5 and 65 thousand
visual.caption: Imagined figures: same average, different distribution.

sections.heading: 4. Comparing states: public facilities
sections.body_md:
Income alone does not show whether people are healthy and educated. Other indicators:
- **Infant mortality rate (IMR):** children who die before the age of one, per 1,000 live births in a year (**lower is better**).
- **Literacy rate:** literate people as a proportion of the population aged **7 and above**.
- **Net attendance ratio:** children of an age group (e.g. 14–15 years) attending school, as a percentage of all children of that age group.

A state with **lower income** can do better on these if it has good **public facilities**: health centres, clean water, schools, midday meals and a well-functioning **public distribution system (PDS)**, whose ration shops supply foodgrains at fair prices. **Kerala** is a well-known example: its income is not the highest, but its infant mortality rate is among the lowest, largely because good basic health care and schooling reach most people.

Some goods and services are best provided **collectively**: security, a pollution-free environment, protection from infectious diseases, schools.

Proportion of literate people in the population aged 7 and above.
Children of an age group attending school as a percentage of all children of that age group.
Government system of ration shops supplying essential foodgrains at fair prices.

sections.heading: 6. Sustainability of development
sections.body_md:
**Sustainable development** meets present needs without reducing the ability of **future generations** to meet theirs.
- **Groundwater** is renewable, but when it is pumped out faster than rain recharges it, the **water table falls** and wells run dry: overuse of a renewable resource.
- **Crude oil** is **non-renewable**: reserves are fixed and will be exhausted at the present rate of use unless new reserves are found. Years the reserves will last = reserves ÷ annual production.
- **Environmental degradation** does not stop at national or state borders, so it is everyone's concern.

Scientists, economists and citizens therefore argue that development must conserve resources and protect the environment.

key_terms.definition_md: Development that meets present needs without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs.
A resource replenished by nature, e.g. groundwater, which can still be overused.
A resource with fixed stocks that is exhausted with use, e.g. crude oil.

- Using average income without its limitation: averages **hide the distribution** of income.
- Answering data questions from the income row only: use **every** indicator.
- Calling groundwater non-renewable: it is **renewable but can be overused**.
- Forgetting units in calculations (₹ per person per year; years).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark MCQ and assertion-reason: one correct option.
- Calculations: formula (or method) + correct answer with unit.
- 3 marks (the economics section has several): three points (about 60 words).
- 5 marks (often data-based in economics): five points that compare figures, interpret them, explain and judge (about 120 words).

**Data in SOYL practice** are imagined but realistic; your board paper will give its own table. Read every row before answering.

questions.stem_md: Why do different people have different development goals?

options.text_md: Because their life situations differ, so what counts as progress for one may not for another
Because only the government can decide what development means
Because development means the same thing for everyone
Because people do not want development

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: People's goals depend on their situation: a landless worker, a farmer and a city student need different things.
Step 2: So (a). (b), (c) and (d) contradict the idea that development is a set of aspirations that vary from person to person.

questions.stem_md: A company wants to build a large factory beside a river to create jobs, while the fishing families downstream want the river to stay clean. This shows that

options.text_md: development goals of different people can conflict
development is only about income
fishing families do not need development
factories never create jobs

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The company's goal (jobs, output) may harm the fishing families' goal (a clean river and their livelihood).
Step 2: One group's progress can be another group's loss, so (a).

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is a **non-material** (non-income) development goal?

options.text_md: A higher salary
A bigger house
Being treated with respect and equality at work
A new car

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Material goals can be bought with money: salary, house, car.
Step 2: Respect, equality, freedom and security are non-material goals that money alone cannot buy, so (c).

questions.stem_md: Meena is offered two jobs: Job 1 pays more but is in a distant city with no job security; Job 2 pays a little less but is near her family, is secure and offers time to study. If Meena chooses Job 2, she is showing that

options.text_md: income is the only thing that matters in a job
people also value goals such as security, family and freedom, not income alone
higher incomes always bring a better life
she does not care about money at all

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: She gives up some income for security, closeness to family and time to study.
Step 2: This shows that development goals include non-income goals, so (b).
Step 3: (d) goes too far: Job 2 still pays well; she is balancing goals.

questions.stem_md: Average income (per capita income) of a country is calculated by

options.text_md: adding the incomes of the richest ten per cent of people
multiplying the total income by the population
dividing the total population by the total income
dividing the total income of the country by its total population

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Per capita income = total income of the country ÷ total population.
Step 2: So (d). (c) inverts the ratio; (a) and (b) are not averages.

questions.stem_md: Why do we use average income rather than total income to compare countries?

options.text_md: Because total income is always secret
Because countries have different populations, so total income does not tell us what an average person earns
Because average income shows how equally income is shared
Because the World Bank does not measure total income

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A large country can have a big total income but a small income per person.
Step 2: Dividing by population makes countries comparable, so (b).
Step 3: (c) is a common mistake: averages **hide** how income is distributed.

questions.stem_md: Two villages have the same average monthly income of ₹20,000 per family. In Village P all four families earn between ₹18,000 and ₹22,000; in Village Q three families earn ₹4,000–₹6,000 and one earns ₹65,000. What does this show?

options.text_md: Both villages are equally developed.
Village Q is more developed because one family is rich.
Averages can hide large inequalities, so they are useful for comparison but not enough on their own.
Average income cannot be calculated for villages.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Both totals are ₹80,000 for four families, so both averages are ₹20,000.
Step 2: Yet in Q most families are poor; the average hides this inequality.
Step 3: So (c). Most people would rather live in P.

questions.stem_md: The World Bank, in classifying countries, uses mainly which criterion?

options.text_md: Literacy rate
Life expectancy
Per capita (average) income
Infant mortality rate

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The World Bank groups countries by income per person (per capita income), into high, middle and low-income groups.
Step 2: So (c). Literacy, life expectancy and infant mortality are used in other measures such as the HDI.

questions.stem_md: In the World Bank's income classification, India is placed among the

options.text_md: high-income countries
upper-middle-income countries
lower-middle-income countries
countries with no classification

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The World Bank groups countries as low, lower-middle, upper-middle and high income by income per person; the thresholds are revised every year.
Step 2: India is a lower-middle-income country, so (c).

questions.stem_md: The infant mortality rate (IMR) of a region tells us

options.text_md: how many children in every 1,000 live births die before completing one year of age
how many children in every 100 attend school
how many people in every 1,000 die in a year
how many mothers die during childbirth

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: IMR counts deaths of babies before their first birthday per 1,000 live births in that year.
Step 2: So (a). (c) describes the overall death rate and (d) maternal mortality.

questions.stem_md: The literacy rate measures

options.text_md: the share of children aged 6–14 enrolled in school
the number of schools per 1,000 people
the share of people aged 7 years and above who can read and write
the share of adults who have passed Class 10

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The literacy rate is the share of people aged seven and above who can read and write.
Step 2: So (c). Enrolment and school counts are different indicators.

questions.stem_md: State Q has a lower per capita income than State P, but a much lower infant mortality rate and a higher literacy rate. What is the most likely reason?

options.text_md: State Q has a colder climate.
State Q provides better public facilities such as health care, schools and a working public distribution system.
People in State Q do not have children.
Per capita income always decides infant mortality.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Money in one's pocket cannot buy everything: clean water, health care and schooling are often provided collectively.
Step 2: A state with good public facilities can have low IMR and high literacy even with a modest income, so (b), as Kerala shows in India.
Step 3: (d) is exactly what the data disprove.

questions.stem_md: Which of these is usually provided better and more cheaply **collectively** than by each family on its own?

options.text_md: A family car
Clothes
Household furniture
Security in the neighbourhood

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Some goods and services are cheaper and better when provided for everyone together: security, a pollution-free environment, protection from infectious diseases, schools.
Step 2: Neighbourhood security is one of them, so (d).

questions.stem_md: The public distribution system (PDS) helps development mainly by

options.text_md: selling luxury goods at high prices
replacing schools in rural areas
raising the incomes of large companies
supplying foodgrains and other essentials at fair prices through ration shops, improving nutrition and health

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Ration shops under the PDS sell rice, wheat and other essentials at controlled prices.
Step 2: Where it works well, people's nutrition and health improve, so (d).

questions.stem_md: Which organisation publishes the Human Development Report that ranks countries by the Human Development Index (HDI)?

options.text_md: The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)
The World Bank
The International Monetary Fund
The World Trade Organization

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The Human Development Report is published by the UNDP.
Step 2: So (a). The World Bank's income classification is a different measure.

questions.stem_md: The Human Development Index combines

options.text_md: per capita income only
exports, imports and foreign exchange
population, area and natural resources
health (life expectancy), education and per capita income

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The HDI measures a long and healthy life (life expectancy at birth), knowledge (schooling) and a decent standard of living (income per person).
Step 2: So (d). It is broader than income alone.

questions.stem_md: Life expectancy at birth means

options.text_md: the number of years a newborn baby is expected to live, on average
the age of the oldest person in a country
the number of years a person spends in school
the age at which people retire

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Life expectancy at birth is the number of years a newborn can expect to live, on average, at current rates of death.
Step 2: So (a).

questions.stem_md: Country L has a higher income per person than Country M, but Country M ranks higher on the Human Development Index. Which explanation fits best?

options.text_md: The HDI ignores income completely.
Country M has better health and education outcomes, which outweigh its lower income in the HDI.
Country L must have a smaller population.
The HDI is calculated only from literacy.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The HDI gives weight to health and education as well as income.
Step 2: A country with longer lives and more schooling can rank above a richer one, so (b).
Step 3: (a) and (d) are false; population size (c) does not decide HDI rank.

questions.stem_md: Development is called **sustainable** when

options.text_md: it raises incomes as fast as possible, whatever the cost
it is planned only by foreign experts
it uses up resources quickly to finish projects early
it meets present needs without reducing the ability of future generations to meet theirs

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Sustainability is about the future as well as the present.
Step 2: Development that keeps resources and the environment healthy for future generations is sustainable, so (d).

questions.stem_md: Groundwater is a renewable resource. Why is its overuse still a threat to sustainable development?

options.text_md: Because groundwater cannot be used for farming
Because when it is drawn faster than rain can recharge it, the water table falls and future users lose it
Because groundwater is a non-renewable resource
Because only factories use groundwater

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A renewable resource is replenished by nature, but only at a certain rate.
Step 2: Using it faster than it is recharged depletes it, so (b).
Step 3: (c) is a common confusion; groundwater is renewable, but it can still be overused.

questions.stem_md: Which of these is a non-renewable resource that will be exhausted after years of use?

options.text_md: Solar energy
Crude oil
Wind
Groundwater

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Crude oil formed over millions of years; reserves are fixed and fall as we use them.
Step 2: So (b). Sun and wind are renewable; groundwater is renewable but can be overused.

questions.stem_md: Why is environmental degradation a concern for every country, not just the one where it happens?

options.text_md: Because pollution and climate effects do not stop at national or state borders
Because every country has the same resources
Because only rich countries pollute
Because international law bans all industry

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Air pollution, river pollution and climate change spread across borders.
Step 2: So sustainability is everyone's concern, (a).

questions.stem_md: The net attendance ratio for an age group compares

options.text_md: the number of schools with the number of teachers
the number of literate adults with the number of children
the marks of boys with the marks of girls
the number of children of that age group attending school with the total number of children in that age group

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The net attendance ratio is the number of children of a given age group (for example 14–15 years) who attend school, as a percentage of all children of that age group.
Step 2: So (d).

questions.stem_md: Which indicator would best show whether a state's **health facilities** are reaching ordinary families?

options.text_md: Per capita income
Number of cars per 1,000 people
Infant mortality rate
Total income of the state

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Infant deaths fall when mothers and babies get good health care, clean water and nutrition.
Step 2: So the IMR is a sensitive measure of health facilities, (c). Income measures do not show whether services reach people.

questions.stem_md: Which Indian state is widely known for having one of the lowest infant mortality rates in the country, largely because of its health and education facilities?

options.text_md: Kerala
Bihar
Uttar Pradesh
Madhya Pradesh

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Kerala has one of the lowest infant mortality rates in India.
Step 2: Good basic health and education facilities explain this, not the highest income. So (a).

questions.stem_md: Which statement about development is most accurate?

options.text_md: Development means only a rise in national income.
Development is the same in every country.
Development cannot be measured in any way.
Development is about improving people's lives, and different people may see it differently.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Development is a set of aspirations for a better life: income, but also health, education, security and freedom.
Step 2: Because people's situations differ, they see development differently. So (d).
Step 3: (a) is too narrow; (b) ignores differences; (c) is false, since income, HDI and other indicators measure it.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Average income is useful for comparing countries.

**Reason (R):** Countries have different populations, so comparing total income alone would be misleading.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is true.
Step 2: R is true and is the reason we divide total income by population. So (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Kerala has one of the lowest infant mortality rates among Indian states.

**Reason (R):** Kerala has the largest area among Indian states.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is true.
Step 2: R is false: Kerala is one of the smaller states; Rajasthan has the largest area. So (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Human Development Index is a broader measure of development than per capita income.

**Reason (R):** The HDI is published by the United Nations Development Programme.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is true: the HDI adds health and education to income.
Step 2: R is true: the UNDP publishes it.
Step 3: Who publishes the index does not explain why it is broader, so (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A family's own income can buy everything it needs to live well.

**Reason (R):** Many important things, such as a pollution-free environment and protection from infectious diseases, are best provided collectively.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is false: some things cannot be bought individually.
Step 2: R is true. So (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Overuse of groundwater threatens sustainable development.

**Reason (R):** When groundwater is drawn faster than rain recharges it, future generations will not have enough.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is true.
Step 2: R is true and explains A: extraction faster than recharge depletes the resource for the future. So (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A landless farm worker and a large landowner may have different development goals.

**Reason (R):** Development goals include both income and non-income goals.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is true: their situations differ, so their goals differ.
Step 2: R is true.
Step 3: But the reason their goals differ is their different life situations, not the fact that goals include income and non-income parts. So (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Average income tells us how income is distributed among the people of a country.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: An average can be the same for an equal and a very unequal society.
Step 2: It hides the distribution, so the statement is false.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The Human Development Report is published by the United Nations Development Programme.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The UNDP publishes the Human Development Report.
Step 2: So the statement is true.

questions.stem_md: True or false? One group's progress can sometimes be another group's loss.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A dam may give electricity to cities but submerge the land of the people living in the valley.
Step 2: Goals can conflict, so the statement is true.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Crude oil is a renewable resource that nature replaces within a few years.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Crude oil took millions of years to form.
Step 2: Its reserves are fixed and fall with use, so it is non-renewable; the statement is false.

questions.stem_md: Total income of a country divided by its total population gives its ___ income.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Total income ÷ population = income per person.
Step 2: The answer is per capita (average) income.

questions.stem_md: The number of children who die before the age of one year, per 1,000 live births in a year, is called the ___ rate.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: This is the definition of IMR.
Step 2: The answer is infant mortality.

questions.stem_md: The index published by the UNDP that combines health, education and income is called the Human ___ Index.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The UNDP ranks countries by the Human Development Index (HDI).
Step 2: The answer is Development.

questions.stem_md: Match each person with the development goal most important to them.

options.text_md: A daily-wage construction worker in a city
A rain-dependent farmer
A young woman from a well-off family
A family in a valley where a dam is planned

match_right.text_md: Freedom to choose her own career and study further
Keeping their land and homes from being flooded
Regular work and fair wages throughout the year
Irrigation and a fair price for crops

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A daily-wage worker needs regular work and fair wages (p–3).
Step 2: A rain-dependent farmer needs irrigation and fair prices (q–4).
Step 3: A young woman from a well-off family may value freedom of choice most (r–1).
Step 4: A valley family facing a dam wants to keep its land and homes (s–2).

questions.stem_md: Countries and states are compared on several development indicators. Match each indicator with what it measures.

options.text_md: Per capita income
Infant mortality rate
Literacy rate
Life expectancy at birth

match_right.text_md: Average number of years a newborn is expected to live
Total income divided by total population
Share of literate people among those aged 7 and above
Deaths before age one per 1,000 live births

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Per capita income = total income ÷ population (p–2).
Step 2: IMR = infant deaths per 1,000 live births (q–4).
Step 3: Literacy rate = literate share of those aged 7+ (r–3).
Step 4: Life expectancy = expected years of life at birth (s–1).

questions.stem_md: Arrange the steps for calculating and using per capita income in the correct order.

options.text_md: Divide the total income by the total population
Find the total income of the country
Compare the result with other countries' per capita income
Find the total population of the country

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: You need the total income first (b), then the population (d).
Step 2: Divide total income by population (a).
Step 3: Only then compare across countries (c).
Step 4: So the order is b, d, a, c.

marking_scheme.step: Correct order b, d, a, c

questions.stem_md: Arrange these steps to show how overuse of groundwater makes development unsustainable.

options.text_md: Wells run dry and future farmers cannot get enough water
Water is pumped out faster than rain can recharge it
More tube wells are dug to irrigate thirsty crops
The water table falls year after year

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: More wells (c) → extraction faster than recharge (b).
Step 2: The water table falls (d).
Step 3: Wells dry up for future users (a).
Step 4: So the order is c, b, d, a.

marking_scheme.step: Correct order c, b, d, a

questions.stem_md: The total annual income of an imagined state is ₹6,00,000 crore and its population is 4 crore. Calculate its per capita income in rupees per year.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Per capita income = total income ÷ population.
Step 2: $\dfrac{600000}{4} = 150000$ (crores cancel).
Step 3: Per capita income = ₹1,50,000 per year.

questions.stem_md: Five families in an imagined village earn ₹12,000, ₹15,000, ₹9,000, ₹30,000 and ₹14,000 a month. What is the average monthly income per family, in rupees?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Total = 12000 + 15000 + 9000 + 30000 + 14000 = 80000.
Step 2: Average = $\dfrac{80000}{5} = 16000$.
Step 3: The average is ₹16,000 a month; note that three of the five families earn less than this.

questions.stem_md: An imagined country has crude oil reserves of 3,600 million barrels and produces 180 million barrels a year. If production stays the same and no new oil is found, for how many years will the reserves last?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Years = reserves ÷ annual production.
Step 2: $\dfrac{3600}{180} = 20$.
Step 3: The reserves will last 20 years.

questions.stem_md:
Map skills (practice). On an outline political map of India, locate and label:

**A.** the state known for one of the lowest infant mortality rates in India.

**B.** the state with the lowest per capita income among Indian states in recent years.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Kerala lies on the south-western coast of India.
Step 2: Bihar lies in the east, in the middle Ganga plain, north of Jharkhand.

marking_scheme.step: A: Kerala correctly located and labelled
B: Bihar correctly located and labelled

questions.stem_md: Give an example to show that the development goals of two groups of people can conflict.

answer.model_answer_md: A new **airport** on the edge of a city gives **jobs and faster travel** to city businesses, but **farmers whose land is acquired** lose their **livelihood and homes**. Development for one group means loss for the other.

questions.solution_md:

questions.passage_md: The imagined country of Kestrava earns most of its export income from crude oil. Its proven reserves are 5,000 million barrels, and it produces 250 million barrels a year. Its planners are debating two choices: **Plan A** — raise production to 500 million barrels a year to earn more now; **Plan B** — keep production steady and invest oil earnings in solar power and schools.

children.stem_md: At the present rate of production, for how many years will Kestrava's reserves last (assuming no new oil is found)?
Under Plan A, for how many years would the reserves last?
**Either** (i): Which plan is more sustainable? Justify your answer.

answer.model_answer_md: **Plan B**. Plan A would **exhaust the oil in 10 years**, leaving future citizens without their main income. Plan B keeps oil for **20 years** and uses its earnings to build **solar power and education**, which will serve **future generations**.

children.solution_md: Compare how long each plan keeps the resource, and what each leaves for the future.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Why can a country that depends heavily on a non-renewable resource face problems in future?

answer.model_answer_md: Its income depends on a resource with **fixed reserves**; when the reserves **run out**, exports and jobs **collapse** unless the country has built **other sources** of income and skills.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined state, per capita income rose by 20 per cent in five years, but the infant mortality rate did not fall at all. What is the most reasonable conclusion?

options.text_md: The state has become fully developed.
Infant mortality cannot be measured accurately.
The extra income has not translated into better health care, nutrition or clean water for ordinary families.
Per capita income always falls when infant mortality is high.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Rising income should make better health possible, but IMR depends on health facilities, nutrition and clean water reaching families.
Step 2: An unchanged IMR suggests the gains are not reaching these services or the families who need them, so (c).
Step 3: (a) ignores the health data; (b) and (d) are unsupported.

questions.stem_md: An imagined town's average monthly income rises from ₹15,000 to ₹18,000 because one factory owner's income jumped, while the wages of all the workers stayed the same. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: Every family in the town is now ₹3,000 a month better off.
The average has risen, but most people are no better off.
The town's income has become more equally distributed.
Average income cannot rise unless every family earns more.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The total rose only because one person's income rose.
Step 2: The average went up, but the workers' incomes did not change, so (b).
Step 3: Inequality has actually increased, so (c) is wrong; (a) and (d) misread what an average is.

questions.stem_md: Which of these actions would make a dry village's use of groundwater more sustainable?

options.text_md: Digging deeper borewells every year
Switching more fields to water-hungry crops
Building check dams and harvesting rainwater to recharge the ground
Pumping water day and night while it lasts

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Sustainable use means extraction should not exceed recharge.
Step 2: Check dams and rainwater harvesting increase recharge, so (c).
Step 3: The other options increase extraction and speed up depletion.

questions.stem_md: An imagined country has oil reserves that will last 20 years at the present rate of production. What happens to the life of the reserves if it halves its production? Show your reasoning.

answer.model_answer_md: Years = reserves ÷ annual production. If production is **halved**, the same reserves are divided by a number **half as large**, so the reserves last **twice as long: 40 years**.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Write the relation: years = reserves ÷ production.
Step 2: Halving the denominator doubles the result: 20 × 2 = 40 years.

questions.stem_md: Why is the infant mortality rate considered a good indicator of the health facilities of a state?

answer.model_answer_md: Babies survive their first year when mothers get **care during pregnancy**, births are **safe**, and babies get **vaccines, nutrition and clean water**. So a **low IMR** shows that basic health services are **reaching ordinary families**.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: List what keeps infants alive.
Step 2: Link these to public health facilities.

marking_scheme.step: Link to health facilities reaching families

questions.stem_md: In an imagined village, the government proposes a higher minimum wage for farm work. Analyse why a large landowner and a landless labourer might disagree about it.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) For the **labourer**, a higher wage means **more income**, better food and schooling for his children: development. (ii) For the **landowner**, it means **higher costs** and lower profits, so he may oppose it. (iii) Their goals **conflict** because their **situations differ**: what is development for one is a loss for the other.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Show the gain for one group.
Step 2: Show the cost for the other.
Step 3: Link to the idea of conflicting goals.

marking_scheme.step: Conflicting goals because of different situations

questions.stem_md: A plan proposes doubling paddy cultivation in a dry district, using tube wells, to raise farmers' incomes quickly. Evaluate the plan from the point of view of sustainability.

answer.model_answer_md: The plan is **not sustainable**. (i) Paddy needs **a lot of water**; in a dry district it would be drawn from **groundwater**. (ii) Pumping **faster than rain recharges** would make the **water table fall** and wells dry up. (iii) Incomes may rise **now** but fall **later**; less thirsty crops and **drip irrigation** would be better.
